records.name: Ilo
records.facts_used: The modern dictionary explanation of Estonian Ilo connects it with ilu, beauty or splendour. An earlier Estonian name collection also gives a joy gloss. These are distinct explanatory records; they should not be merged into one translation or automatically replaced with the history of Finnish ilo. Julius Mägiste’s 1929 Eestipäraseid isikunimesid places Ilo in the women’s list with German Freude, Freudebringerin, joy or bringer of joy. Official Estonian statistics at the start of 2026 record Ilo among both men and women. The historical women’s list therefore does not delimit all later use.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete dated dictionary, calendar, press or historical record support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: Exact Estonian Wiktionary section derives Ilo from ilu beauty/splendour. Visually checked Mägiste PDF p. 15 / printed p. 13, feminine list: Ilo (Rnm., = freude, freudebringerin). Preserve the distinct historical joy gloss without inventing one merged meaning or assuming the Finnish route. The next line is Ilts-u, not Ilu. Opened Statistics Estonia exact ILO page confirms 23 men and 15 women on 1 January 2026; narrative only says both sexes. Publication 1929 is not coining. Modern dictionary masculine label does not negate historical and official female use. The inherited same-spelling Latvian record is separate: opened LV-SILINS p. 161 lists thirteenth-century Ikšķile / third-quarter-twentieth-century Cēsis and warns against combining them without a gender distinction. It does not date the Estonian name. Fixed the date formatter so a later slash-separated record cannot lend its quarter to the earlier century; preserved raw text and Latvian scope.

records.name: Ginvydas
records.facts_used: Ginvydas is a Lithuanian two-stem name. The name guide connects gin- with ginti, to defend, and vyd- with (iš)vydo, saw. These explain separate elements; they need not be turned into an invented literal sentence about the bearer’s character. An ELTA calendar dispatch dated 16 November 2010 lists both Ginvydas and Ginvydė for the day after tomorrow, 18 November. This is a dated press record of both forms in the calendar. Its publication year does not date the names’ creation or first registration.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete dated dictionary, calendar, press or historical record support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: Exact LT-GUIDE gives gin- ginti/gina and vyd- (iš)vydo. ELTA dispatch dated 16 November 2010 explicitly lists Ginvydas and Ginvydė in the poryt (two days later, 18 November) list. This dated press/calendar evidence is not a first registration or coining date. Salys contains related Gin(t)- analyses but no exact Ginvydas entry was found, so no related name’s dates are transferred. Commercial generated-looking bearer biographies were rejected without primary confirmation. Direct ELTA HTML fetch returned 403; the web reader successfully opened the full dated text.

records.name: Otas
records.facts_used: Otas belongs to the Germanic Odo, Oto and Otto family. Its basis is associated with Old High German ot, wealth or possessions. The Lithuanian guide explains Otas within this family; resemblance to a word in another language does not itself establish another origin. The 1964 Tikiu Dievą calendar lists Otonas with short form Otas on 2 July. The list was reprinted in volume two of Salys’s writings in 1983. This historical calendar page directly documents their relationship, although its date differs from the calendar used here.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete dated dictionary, calendar, press or historical record support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: LT-GUIDE and curated Otto establish Germanic Odo/Oto/Otto, Old High German ot wealth. Visually checked Salys PDF p. 310 / printed p. 295: LIEPA heading, day 2, Otonas (Otas). This is 2 JULY in the 1964 calendar reprinted 1983, not 30 June suggested by nearby extracted context and not the project’s 18 November. Preserve supplied calendar dates; this historical page proves the spelling bridge only.

records.name: Otonas
records.facts_used: The Lithuanian guide explains Otonas as related to Otas, or Odas. This is a Germanic name family with a basis meaning wealth or possessions. The explicit pairing Otonas (Otas) in a historical calendar also documents the connection in a concrete name list. Visuotinė lietuvių enciklopedija explicitly pairs Lithuanian Otonas I with Otto I. He was a German ruler and Holy Roman emperor from 962 to 973. This encyclopaedic example shows the Lithuanian name form in European history, rather than a Lithuanian ruler or the first bearer in Lithuania.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete dated dictionary, calendar, press or historical record support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: LT-GUIDE explicitly relates Otonas to Otas/Odas. Visually checked Salys PDF p. 310 / printed p. 295 directly pairs Otonas (Otas) on 2 July. Opened LT-VLE explicitly pairs Otonas I with Otto I, German ruler and Holy Roman emperor 962–973. It is a foreign historical figure in Lithuanian translation, not a Lithuanian ruler or an attestation of domestic first use. Unsupported popular Greek-ear derivation rejected.

records.name: Romanas
records.facts_used: Romanas is connected with Latin Romanus, a Roman, referring to Rome and the Roman world. The Lithuanian guide and international Roman name family support this explanation. The modern common noun romanas, a novel, does not itself explain the personal name’s origin. The dictionary appendix in the 1983 second volume of Salys’s writings explicitly pairs Romanas with Roman(us). It also lists Romas as a short form of both Romanas and Romualdas. This concrete dictionary record shows why a shared short form need not identify one particular full name.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete dated dictionary, calendar, press or historical record support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: LT-GUIDE and curated Roman give Latin Romanus, a Roman. Visually checked Salys PDF p. 263 / printed p. 248: exact Romanas → Roman(us); Romas short for both Romanas and Romualdas. Publication 1983 is not first use. Common noun romanas and Romas-only biographies do not establish a Romanas bearer.

records.name: Dolita
records.facts_used: Siliņš’s dictionary places Dolita in the English Dolly and Doroteja family. Its basis is Greek dōron, gift, and theos, god. The short form is thus explained through the history of the full name; resemblance to Doloresa alone does not establish another origin. The dictionary places an example of Dolita in Alūksne in the third quarter of the twentieth century. This geographically and chronologically located record shows the form in Latvian use. The source does not give a precise creation year or a separate year of calendar inclusion.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete dated dictionary, calendar, press or historical record support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: LV-SILINS pp. 100–101 places Dolita under English Dolly/Doroteja, Greek dōron/theos. Exact Dolita record: Alūksne, third quarter of the twentieth century; no calendar-entry year. Curated Dolly corroborates Dorothy short-form tradition, but its additional modern Dolores use does not override the exact catalogue link.

records.name: Doloresa
records.facts_used: Doloresa is connected with Latin dolor, pain or sorrow. In the international name family, Spanish Dolores is the plural meaning sorrows and belongs to the Marian title Nuestra Señora de los Dolores. This explains the religious naming tradition without establishing a single route into Latvia. Klāvs Siliņš’s dictionary dates a personal-name record of Doloresa to 1930 and calendar inclusion to 1964. These are separate records of use and later calendar membership, rather than a date when the name was invented.
records.reason: Opened exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete dated dictionary, calendar, press or historical record support the five-language narrative.
records.uncertainties: LV-SILINS p. 100: Latin dolor, personal record 1930 and calendar 1964. Curated Dolores documents Spanish plural sorrows and the Marian title Nuestra Señora de los Dolores; this is family context, not a uniquely demonstrated transmission into Latvia.

The dictionary places a personal-name record of Laisve in the second quarter of the twentieth century and dates its calendar entry to 1931. The broader period is not an exact birth date for a first bearer. These details distinguish usage history from calendar history.

records.uncertainties: LV-SILINS p. 206: Lithuanian laisvė freedom; exact Latvian spelling Laisve, personal record second quarter of the twentieth century, calendar 1931. Preserve e rather than silently substituting Lithuanian ė.

records.name: Latvis

The meaning therefore belongs to the Latvian self-designation rather than to a similar-sounding personal name in another language. The dictionary records Latvis in a calendar as early as 1902, while dating a personal-name record to 1942. In this source the calendar proposal precedes the cited bearer record. The year 1942 does not prove that the name was created only then.

records.uncertainties: LV-SILINS p. 209: Latvian latvis, a Latvian; calendar 1902, personal record 1942. Calendar proposal and bearer record are separate.
